title: React Forms & Validation
description: An interactive course on React forms — controlled and uncontrolled components, validation strategies, and handling user input effectively.
content:
React forms: choose who owns the value

A form starts with browser behavior: an input has a value, the browser can validate it, and submit attempts to send it. React adds another possible owner of that value. The key design question is not “which hook do I use?” but “which layer needs to read or change this value, and when?”

Controlled inputs

A controlled input receives its current value from React state and reports edits through an event. React is the source of truth. This makes conditional UI, live formatting, dependent fields, and immediate validation straightforward, but every edit causes state updates and the input must stay controlled for its whole lifetime.

const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
<input
  type="email"
  value={email}
  onChange={(event) => setEmail(event.target.value)}
/>

On each keystroke, the browser emits an input event; the handler reads the new string; the state setter schedules a render; and the next render passes that value back to the input. If you omit onChange, the displayed value cannot be edited. If the value starts as undefined and later becomes a string, React warns that the input changed from uncontrolled to controlled. Initialize text fields with an empty string, not undefined.

Uncontrolled inputs

With an uncontrolled input, the DOM keeps the current value. Use a ref when React needs a particular value, or FormData in the submit handler when reading the whole form. This can reduce state plumbing for a simple form, but React will not automatically re-render dependent UI as the user types.

function handleSubmit(event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
  const email = String(data.get('email') ?? '');
}

Do not mix the models accidentally: an input should use either value/onChange or defaultValue/ref, not both as competing sources of truth.

Validation is layered, not a security boundary

Native HTML constraints such as required, type="email", min, max, and minLength provide useful browser feedback and expose validity through the Constraint Validation API. By default, an invalid form does not dispatch its submit event; the browser focuses a failing control and presents its own message. If you add noValidate, you opt out of that automatic submit blocking and must implement the equivalent checks yourself.

Client-side validation improves feedback, but it can be bypassed. The server must validate every submitted value and enforce authorization. Validation also does not prevent SQL injection or cross-site scripting: use parameterized database queries, context-appropriate output encoding, and server-side security controls.

Custom validation and timing

Custom rules are useful for relationships the browser cannot express, such as matching password fields or a date range. Showing an error on every keystroke can be noisy; waiting until submit can hide a fixable problem. A common pattern is to show a field error after it has been blurred once or after a submit attempt, then re-check it on later edits. This is a choice, not a universal rule: test keyboard use, screen-reader announcements, and how disruptive the feedback feels.

const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
const [touched, setTouched] = useState(false);
const emailError =
  touched && !/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(email)
    ? 'Enter a valid email address.'
    : '';

<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input
  id="email"
  type="email"
  value={email}
  onChange={(event) => setEmail(event.target.value)}
  onBlur={() => setTouched(true)}
  aria-invalid={Boolean(emailError)}
  aria-describedby={emailError ? 'email-error' : undefined}
/>
{emailError && <p id="email-error">{emailError}</p>

Associate each control with a visible label. Connect its error with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid only when it is invalid. On submit, focus the first invalid field or provide a summary that links to invalid controls. Do not rely on color alone.

Walkthrough: submit, validate, then report

  1. The browser first applies native constraints unless the form uses noValidate.
  2. For a valid submission, React receives the submit event. Call preventDefault to stop a page navigation when the app handles the request itself.
  3. Run cross-field and domain rules. Keep errors next to the fields they describe.
  4. Set a submitting state before awaiting the request; disable duplicate submission and announce progress accessibly.
  5. Handle server field errors, network failure, and success as distinct outcomes. A client check can never guarantee that the server will accept the data.
  6. In finally, clear the submitting state. Preserve entered values after recoverable failures so the learner does not have to retype them.

Debug a form by inspecting the actual submit event and its defaultPrevented value, checking input.value and input.validity in DevTools, and looking at the Network panel. Confirm whether a request was sent, whether the server returned a validation error, and whether the UI translated that response into useful feedback.

When a form library helps

React Hook Form can reduce rerendering and repetitive registration/error wiring, especially for larger forms. It commonly uses uncontrolled fields and refs internally; Controller adapts controlled third-party widgets. A schema resolver can share domain rules, but browser and server validation still have separate responsibilities.

A library adds concepts, bundle weight, and another API to debug. For a small form with a few fields, native constraints and a small amount of React state may be clearer. Choose based on field count, conditional sections, validation complexity, accessibility requirements, and team familiarity—not on the assumption that every form needs a library.

Practice: build a registration form

Implement name, email, password, and confirm-password fields. Use controlled values for any field that drives live UI; choose intentionally for the rest. Keep the server response simulated, but make loading, success, and recoverable error states visible.

  • Use semantic form markup, associated labels, appropriate input types, and autocomplete tokens.
  • Require a name, validate email format, and require the two passwords to match.
  • Do not announce untouched-field errors immediately; after blur or submit, update feedback as the learner edits.
  • Prevent duplicate submits, show a pending state, and preserve values on simulated network failure.
  • Explain in a short note which fields are controlled and why, and what validation the server must repeat.

Success criteria

  • A keyboard-only user can identify every field, error, and submit status.
  • Invalid data is blocked with actionable feedback; the first invalid field can be found without guessing.
  • Valid data produces one request; pending, failure, and success states are distinguishable.
  • Changing a value cannot leave a stale error visible after the value becomes valid.
  • The implementation does not claim client validation makes untrusted input safe.

Debugging challenge

A submit handler never runs, even though its button is clicked. Inspect the form’s native validity state first: a required field or type constraint may be blocking submission before React receives the event. Then check whether noValidate was added and whether custom validation now covers the rules you still need.
